title: The Wrong Cargo: Where the Idea Came From
body:
Crime fiction runs on logistics — who has the thing, who wants it, how far it has to travel. I wanted a cargo so wrong that every ordinary decision became impossible. A dinosaur skeleton in a stolen removals van, crossing three counties, with people who cannot call the police, was the answer.

The comedy is not in the dinosaur. It is in watching competent-ish adults discover, one motel at a time, that there is no correct next move.

title: Dark Comedy Only Works If the Danger Is Real
body:
Funny crime fails when the threat is decorative. The reader has to believe someone could genuinely die, or the jokes float free of consequence. The cartel in the title is not a punchline; it is the reason the characters keep making worse choices at speed.

The craft balance is tonal: the narration can be dry, the dialogue can be sharp, but the violence, when it lands, is written straight.

title: Road Stories and the Pleasure of the Next Bad Idea
body:
A road novel is a sequence of rooms — motels, forecourts, laybys — each with its own small cast and its own way of going wrong. The structure is episodic by nature, so the engine has to be character: what will these particular people do when the map runs out?

The answer, reliably, is something worse and more human than the plan. That is the story.
